title: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
shortTitle: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
summary: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage moves collected data into a consumer or enterprise file service such as Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive or Box instead of sending it over the primary command and control channel. Many clients synchronise automatically, so a file copied into a synced folder leaves the network without any explicit upload command, and the resulting traffic is HTTPS to a well known domain. Artefacts include the desktop sync client appearing on a host that never had it, new device authorisations on a corporate tenant, browser sessions to personal storage accounts, large uploads attributed to an unfamiliar account, bulk creation of shared links, and files archived or renamed immediately before transfer. Attackers often stage the data with compression or encryption first, which shows as archive creation followed by a burst of outbound volume. Defenders separate this from legitimate activity by knowing which storage tenants the organisation sanctions, tying uploads to an identity, and watching for personal accounts and anonymous share links from managed hosts.

beginner.definition: Exfiltration over a web service means sending stolen data out through a normal internet service. This version uses an online file storage service, such as Dropbox or Google Drive. The upload travels as ordinary encrypted web traffic, so it blends in with daily work. The attacker can then open the files from anywhere.
beginner.whyItMatters: Cloud storage is a normal part of modern work, so you cannot simply block all of it. Attackers exploit that fact. Data leaves through a trusted path and lands in an account that you do not control. Without clear rules about which storage services are allowed and who may use them, a large data theft can look just like routine file sharing.
howItWorks: The attacker gains a user account, or installs the desktop sync client on a compromised machine.
They collect the interesting files and often put them into one archive to make the transfer simpler.
They copy the archive into a synced folder, or they upload it through the service's web page.
The sync client sends the data in the background, so nobody has to watch the transfer happen.
They may create a public sharing link so that other machines can collect the same data later.
Cleanup follows, with the local archive deleted to remove the most obvious clue.
beginner.example: Imagine a block of flats with a shared parcel room. Anyone with a key can leave a box there in the morning and collect it later through a different entrance. A thief does not need to carry your belongings out of the front door; he leaves them in the parcel room and picks them up when the hall is quiet. Uploading to cloud storage is that same trick, using a room that the whole company already has a key to.
takeaways: Decide which cloud storage services are approved, and treat personal accounts on work machines as a warning sign.
A file placed in a synced folder leaves the network without any obvious upload command from the user.
Large outbound transfers to storage services should be tied to a named person and a business reason.

objectives: Explain how cloud storage synchronisation can exfiltrate data without a visible upload step.
Identify the identity, client and network artefacts that this activity leaves behind.
Describe how to tell an approved storage service from a personal account used for theft.
Explain why data staging with archives or encryption often precedes the transfer.
Describe controls that limit exfiltration while still allowing legitimate file sharing.
